uslaw-usc-t2-s141b:
Section 141b of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the goods of the Library of Congress and with order in its halls. It sits in Chapter 5, on the Library of Congress. The Librarian of Congress is to set the marks and rules for the safety of the Library's sets and goods. Those rules also cover the charge of the Library and the keep of good order and fair conduct in its rooms.

A second clause deals with the care of the systems of safety. It names the Chief of the Capitol Police and the Librarian of Congress as the men in charge of those systems. Their charge rests on the powers set by the act that made the section, and on the laws the text names. The part of the text shown here is cut off at the start of that clause.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1881b: Section 1881b of Title 2 of the United States Code orders rules for the Capitol flown flags plan for families of fallen heroes. Within thirty days after May 16, 2016, the Architect of the Capitol had to issue those rules. The rules must set the steps to ask for such a flag, with forms, guides, and papers to go with it. The rules take effect only on approval by the House Administration Committee and the Senate Rules and Administration Committee.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1901b:
Section 1901b of Title 2 of the United States Code authorizes joint oversight hearings on the Capitol Police. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the Capitol Police chapter, on organization and administration. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. Two committees, one from each house, act together.

The Senate Committee on Rules and Administration and the House Administration Committee are the named pair, the text states. They are authorized to jointly conduct oversight hearings on the matters the section specifies. Joint hearings mean the force that guards both houses answers to both houses at one table. Duplicated probes and split messages are avoided by design.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1b: Section 1b of Title 2 adds a countersignature to an election paper. The certificate mentioned in the prior section of the title must be countersigned by the secretary of state of the State. The section sits in Chapter 1 of Title 2, on the election of Senators and Representatives. The hosted Code text is published by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel, current through Public Law 119-134. One line, and a State officer's signature becomes part of a federal credential.
uslaw-usc-t2-s281b:
Section 281b of Title 2 of the United States Code lists functions of an office. The office is the House Office of Legislative Counsel, which drafts bills. The first function deals with managers for the House at a joint conference. On request, the office must advise and aid those managers there.

The aid runs through the course of the conference on split votes. It takes in help with the conference report and its notes. The second function deals with panels of the House that ask for aid. The office must advise them as they weigh bills before them. It helps them draw up drafts of bills, changes, and reports. The third function puts staff of the office on the House floor. Not more than two staff may attend a Member in charge of time. They aid that Member while a bill is weighed on the floor.
uslaw-usc-t2-s661b:
Section 661b of Title 2 of the United States Code assigns the estimating work for federal credit programs. It sits in the credit reform subchapter, which governs direct loans and loan guarantees. Sound budgets need agreed estimates of what such loans will cost.

For the executive branch, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget runs the estimates. He is responsible for coordinating the estimates the subchapter requires. He must consult the agencies that run the loan and guarantee programs. The Director may hand estimating authority to those agencies. Any such delegation must rest on written guidelines, regulations, or criteria. Those standards must stay consistent with the subchapter's definitions. A further part coordinates the work with the Congressional Budget Office. The section keeps two budget offices, executive and legislative, working from matched figures.
